blocks.text: When people talk about language we realize that the discussion generally reveals a number of legends, popular beliefs and prejudices which confuse the issue and obscure the facts. Everybody uses language and so everybody feels himself an expert on the subject. In particular most people have an irrational but understandable feeling that what they themselves do is in some way «right» or «good», and that anything different is in some way inferior or unacceptable. As a consequence of these myths and prejudices, many people are worried by the idea that there exists a single kind of English, «good English» and that any spoken or written English should follow its rules.

In Venezuela there is quite a large number of people who equate this notion of «good English» to British English. This leads them to express opinions, such as «British English is better than American English», «British English is more beautiful», «The English are the only people who speak good English», «Americans don’t speak English». It is often hard to convince them that though there are some differences between the several varieties of the English language, none of them is intrinsically superior to the others.
Every variety of English, as any other language, has a so called standard form, which is spoken by the educated section of the population that usually belongs to a particular social group.
All languages unavoidably change as time passes and English is no exception. That is why today’s English is different from Shakespeare’s. And the change continues, inevitably.

In conclusion, we must keep in mind that judgements that British English is «better» or «worse» than American English are prejudices without any basis in the description of language. We must also accept changes that occur in all languages and forget common legends about language which hinder a clear understanding of what language is and how it functions.
Decide whether the following statements are TRUE or FALSE.

items.q: Some languages are better than others.
Venezuelan Spanish is not as good as European Spanish.
The standard form of a language is ordinarily spoken by people who have attended school.
The British are not the best speakers of the English language.
We must prefer British English becuase it is the best of all varieties of this language.

blocks.title: Carlos Would Like to Get Some Answers From Professor Taylor

blocks.text: Carlos Fernández, a student taking courses in linguistics and the teaching of English as a foreing language, is talking with Professor Ronald Taylor, visiting lecturer at Caracas Teachers’ College.

items: *R.T.:* Let’s see, Carlos. You said you wanted to see me. Is there something I can do for you?
*C.F.:* Yes, sir. I’d like to ask you some questions about the differences, if there are any, between British and American English.
*R.T.:* Well, there are certainly some differences between the two forms of the same language.
*C.F.:* I’ve heard people say that British English is better than American English; that the British speak good English; that American English is in some way inferior.

*R.T.:* Such judgements are based on popular myths. Most people share a number of prejudices about what language is and how it should be taught. In the present case neither is better or worse; they’re just a little different.
*C.F.:* But I’ve often felt kind of confused. As you know some of our teachers here are British and others are Americans. What kind of English am I supposed to learn or to imitate?

*R.T.:* If I were you, I’d try to acquire *one* pronunciation; that is, I’d try to speak as the Americans or as the English, depending on my personal preference or needs. But remember that you should also try to understand other forms of English.
*C.F.:* Could you please tell me a little more about the differences?

*R.T.:* To satisfy your curiosity I’ll give you a few examples: In pronuciation: In the U.S.A. the word fork is pronounced /fork/ while in England it is pronounced /fok/. In grammar: In the U.S.A., people say, do you have a match?, while in England this question doesn’t take the auxiliary *do;* and they ask, have you a match? In vocabulary: In the U.S.A. «we *rent* a car»; whereas in England «we *hire* a car». In spelling: In American English we write *center, traveled, organize,* but the British write *centre, travelled, organise.*
*R.T.:* There’s nothing to worry about. In spite of these differences, the Americans and the English understand each other very well. They share a common language and that’s a fact.
*C.F.:* Thank you, Professor Taylor. I’ve learned a lot from your explanations.
*R.T.:* You’re welcome. Feel free to come any time you need some help.
